## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 23: Applications: Infer](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inference-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to carry a real experiment on redundant adjectives through the computational methods of inference, a bootstrap confidence interval for one mean, a randomization test for paired means, and randomization tests for two independent means, checking each against the $t$-distribution.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `applications-infer`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. You may need to restart this tutorial after you do so.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Applications: Infer"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

## A confidence interval for one mean

"Bootstrapping, in contrast to randomization tests, represents a proxy sampling of the original population." This section turns the study's 880 answers into one percentage per speaker and display, then bootstraps a confidence interval for the mean of one group, as the chapter does.

### Exercise 1

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question("In the bash Terminal, run head data/redundant_adjectives.csv. CP/CR.", type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
Language,Subject,Question,Color Response
English,1,1,1
English,1,2,1
English,1,3,1
English,1,4,1
English,1,5,1
English,1,6,1
English,1,7,1
English,1,8,1
English,1,9,1
```

###

The file has no help page, so the chapter is its documentation: researchers "showed the following two images to 22 native English speakers (undergraduates from University College London) and 22 native Spanish speakers (undergraduates from the Universidad de las Islas Baleares)." A `Color Response` of 1 means the speaker said "the blue triangle" when "the triangle" was enough, a redundant adjective.

English speakers used a redundant adjective in 37.3% of 4-item displays and 80.5% of 16-item displays, Spanish speakers in 2.7% and 61.4%. ### Exercise 10

Replace the code in that chunk so that it creates `boot_eng_4`, the means of 1,000 bootstrap resamples of `redundant_perc` for English speakers with 4-item displays. Set the seed to 74 first, as the chapter's code does. Print `boot_eng_4`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-10-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(74)
boot_eng_4 <- redundant |>
  filter(language == "English", items == 4) |>
  specify(response = redundant_perc) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_eng_4
```

###

Each row is the mean of one resample: "Repeatedly resample the original data, with replacement, using the same sample size as the original data." "With bootstrapping, the analyst is not forcing the null hypothesis to be true (or false, for that matter), but instead, they are replicating the variability seen in taking repeated samples from a population."

````{verbatim}
set.seed(74)
boot_eng_4 <- redundant |>
  filter(language == "English", items == 4) |>
  specify(response = redundant_perc) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")
````

###

The seed fixes the 1,000 resamples, so every render gives the same interval. "Because there is no underlying true (or false) null hypothesis, bootstrapping is typically used for creating confidence intervals for the parameter of interest."

### Exercise 15

The chapter's recap describes a second bootstrap interval: "The confidence interval will be given by the original observed statistic plus or minus some multiple (e.g., 2) of SEs." Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates the observed mean for English speakers with 4-item displays, the standard deviation of the bootstrap means as the SE, and the interval from the mean minus 2 SEs to the mean plus 2 SEs. Render.

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-15
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-15-test
#| echo: true
redundant |>
  filter(language == "English", items == 4) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(redundant_perc)) |>
  mutate(se = sd(boot_eng_4$stat),
         lower = mean - 2 * se,
         upper = mean + 2 * se)
```

###

The SE interval, 17.1% to 57.4%, is a little wider than the percentile interval and centered exactly on the observed 37.3%. "Bootstrap percentile interval: Obtain the endpoints representing the middle (e.g., 95%) of the bootstrapped statistics."

### Exercise 16

Check the bootstrap against the mathematical model. Replace the code in that chunk with a 95% confidence interval for the same mean from the $t$-distribution, done by a single function built for it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-16
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-16-test
#| echo: true
redundant |>
  filter(language == "English", items == 4) |>
  t_test(response = redundant_perc, conf_level = 0.95)
```

###

The $t$-interval, 15.7% to 58.8% on 21 degrees of freedom, is wider still, and its conditions are shaky: "slight skew is okay for sample sizes of 15, moderate skew for sample sizes of 30, and strong skew for sample sizes of 60," and these 22 values sit in two clumps at 0 and 100. "Second, when there is a difference in the conclusions (seen primarily in methods beyond the scope of this text), it is often the case that the computational method relies on fewer technical conditions and is therefore more appropriate to use."

### Exercise 17

Replace the code in that chunk with a histogram of the 1,000 bootstrap means in `boot_eng_4`, with vertical lines at the two ends of the 95% percentile interval. Render.

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-17
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: a-confidence-interval-for-one-mean-17-test
#| echo: true
ci_eng_4 <- boot_eng_4 |>
  get_confidence_interval(level = 0.95, type = "percentile")

boot_eng_4 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_eng_4$lower_ci, ci_eng_4$upper_ci))
```

###

The bootstrap means pile up around 37 even though no single English speaker scored anywhere near 37. Averaging 22 speakers smooths two clumps into one hump, which is why a mean can have a well-behaved bootstrap distribution when the data do not.

"However, these confidence intervals are not very meaningful to compare to one another as the interpretation of the "true mean redundant adjective usage percentage" is quite an abstract concept." Comparisons, between display sizes and between languages, call for hypothesis tests.

###

A confidence interval for one mean takes three steps by bootstrap: resample, recompute the mean, and keep the middle 95%. The same steps work for a median or any other statistic, which is why the bootstrap is the more general tool even when the $t$-interval agrees with it.

## Testing paired and independent means

"An important feature of randomization tests is that the data are permuted in such a way that the null hypothesis is true." This section runs the chapter's two kinds of test: a paired test comparing each English speaker with themselves, and independent-means tests comparing English speakers with Spanish speakers.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that keeps only the English speakers in `redundant` and reshapes them so that each speaker is one row, with their 4-item and 16-item percentages in two columns, `perc_4` and `perc_16`. Add a column `diff`, the 16-item percentage minus the 4-item percentage. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-1-test
#| echo: true
redundant |>
  filter(language == "English") |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = subject, names_from = items,
              names_prefix = "perc_", values_from = redundant_perc) |>
  mutate(diff = perc_16 - perc_4)
```

###

"Note that the English speaking participants were each evaluated on both the 4 item and the 16 item displays." "Therefore, the variable of interest is the difference in redundant percentage."

```{r}
  pivot_wider(id_cols = subject, names_from = items,
```

Eleven speakers did not change at all, and all 11 who did change used more redundant adjectives with 16 items, by 70 to 100 points. Not one English speaker went the other way.

### Exercise 4

Replace the mean so that the code creates `null_eng`, the mean differences from 1,000 shuffles under the null hypothesis that display size makes no difference, shuffling each speaker's two percentages between the displays. Set the seed to 74 first. Print `null_eng`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-4-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(74)
null_eng <- redundant |>
  filter(language == "English") |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = subject, names_from = items,
              names_prefix = "perc_", values_from = redundant_perc) |>
  mutate(diff = perc_16 - perc_4) |>
  specify(response = diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

null_eng
```

###

The paired test "shuffles the observed percentage across the two groups (4 item vs 16 item) but **within** a single participant." Swapping a speaker's two percentages just flips the sign of their difference, so each shuffle is a random choice of plus or minus for each of the 22 differences.

### Exercise 5

Replace the line that prints `null_eng` with one that calculates the mean, the smallest, and the largest of the 1,000 shuffled mean differences. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-5-test
#| echo: true
null_eng |>
  summarize(mean = mean(stat), min = min(stat), max = max(stat))
```

###

"Note that the distribution is centered at 0, since the structure of randomly assigning redundancy percentages to each item display will balance the data out such that the average of any differences will be zero." Our shuffles ranged from -43.18 to 36.8: none reached the observed 43.18, and just one matched it in the other direction.

### Exercise 6

Replace that line with one that calculates the p-value: the proportion of shuffles whose mean difference is at least as far from 0 as the observed 43.18, in either direction. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-6-test
#| echo: true
null_eng |>
  summarize(p_value = mean(abs(stat) >= 43.18))
```

###

Our p-value is 0.001, one shuffle in 1,000, and the chapter reports "a p-value that is approximately 0." With all 11 nonzero differences positive, the observed 43.18 is the most extreme mean a shuffle can produce, so the exact p-value is 2 in $2^{11}$, about 0.001.

### Exercise 7

Check the randomization test against the mathematical model. Replace the code in that chunk with a paired $t$-test of `diff` against a null value of 0, done by a single function built for it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-7-test
#| echo: true
redundant |>
  filter(language == "English") |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = subject, names_from = items,
              names_prefix = "perc_", values_from = redundant_perc) |>
  mutate(diff = perc_16 - perc_4) |>
  t_test(response = diff, mu = 0)
```

###

The $t$-test gives T = 4.48 on 21 degrees of freedom and a p-value of 0.0002, the same conclusion as the shuffles. "With such a small p-value, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the data provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean redundant adjective usage percentages across different displays for English speakers."

### Exercise 9

Change the code so that, after setting the seed to 74, it shuffles the language labels among the 44 speakers 1,000 times, calculates the difference in means for each shuffle, and returns the two-sided p-value for the observed difference of 34.5. Render.

Our p-value is 0.114, where the chapter's own code, with the same seed, gets 0.102: six shuffles tie the observed 19.09 exactly, but rounding inside the computer made them a hair smaller, so a cutoff of exactly 19.09 misses them. Either way, "the data provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean redundant adjective usage percentages between languages in 4 item displays (small p-value) but not in 16 item displays (not small p-value)."

### Exercise 11

Check both language comparisons against the mathematical model. Replace the code in that chunk with a two-sample $t$-test, English minus Spanish, for each display size, with the two results stacked in one table and labeled by display size. Render.

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: testing-paired-and-independent-means-11-test
#| echo: true
bind_rows(
  "4 items" = redundant |>
    filter(items == 4) |>
    t_test(redundant_perc ~ language, order = c("English", "Spanish")),
  "16 items" = redundant |>
    filter(items == 16) |>
    t_test(redundant_perc ~ language, order = c("English", "Spanish")),
  .id = "display"
)
```

###

The $t$-tests give p-values of 0.003 and 0.094, against our 0.002 and 0.114 by simulation, so the two methods reach the same conclusions. "For a difference of means when the data are not paired: each sample mean must separately satisfy the one-sample conditions for the $t$-distribution, and the data in the groups must also be independent."

Two gaps show at once: the rise from 4 to 16 items within each language, which the paired test confirmed for English, and the gap between the languages, which is wide with 4 items and narrower with 16. Treating `items` as a category keeps the axis from inventing display sizes between 4 and 16.


###

```{.output}
a8d4f17 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Test paired and independent means
5c21e0a Bootstrap a confidence interval
9be04d2 Initial commit
```

###

"In approaching research questions with a randomization test, be sure to ask yourself what the null hypothesis represents and how it is that permuting the data is creating different possible null data representations." The paired test shuffled within each speaker and the language tests shuffled across speakers, because the null hypotheses were different.

###

Every test in this section followed the same recipe: compute the observed statistic, shuffle the data so that the null hypothesis is true, recompute, and see how often the shuffles are as extreme. Only the shuffle changes with the design of the study, and choosing it correctly is the part no software can do for you.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 23: Applications: Infer](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inference-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to carry a real experiment on redundant adjectives through the computational methods of inference, a bootstrap confidence interval for one mean, a randomization test for paired means, and randomization tests for two independent means, checking each against the $t$-distribution.

For the study itself, read "[Speakers and listeners exploit word order for communicative efficiency: A cross-linguistic investigation](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000963)" by Paula Rubio-Fernandez, Francis Mollica, and Julian Jara-Ettinger, whose data the authors share on the [Open Science Framework](https://osf.io/9hw68/). For more practice with this part of the book, the chapter points to OpenIntro's [Tutorial 5: Statistical inference](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims-tutorials/05-infer/).

````{verbatim}
```{r}
redundant <- read_csv("data/redundant_adjectives.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(language = Language, subject = Subject,
         question = Question, color_response = `Color Response`) |>
  mutate(items = if_else(question > 10, 16, 4)) |>
  summarize(redundant_perc = sum(color_response) * 100 / n(),
            .by = c(language, subject, items))
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
set.seed(74)
boot_eng_4 <- redundant |>
  filter(language == "English", items == 4) |>
  specify(response = redundant_perc) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")
```

```{r}
ci_eng_4 <- boot_eng_4 |>
  get_confidence_interval(level = 0.95, type = "percentile")

boot_eng_4 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_eng_4$lower_ci, xmax = ci_eng_4$upper_ci,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_eng_4$lower_ci, ci_eng_4$upper_ci),
             color = "navy") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Redundant Adjectives Among English Speakers, 4-Item Displays",
       subtitle = "95% confidence interval for the mean usage: 19.1% to 56.4%",
       x = "Mean Percentage of Answers With a Redundant Adjective",
       y = "Number of Bootstrap Resamples",
       caption = "22 English speakers, 1,000 bootstrap resamples\nRubio-Fernandez, Mollica, and Jara-Ettinger (2021), via Introduction to Modern Statistics")
```
````
